projects.title: Anyday Website
projects.summary: A new website for Anyday that sells what it actually does: one web platform that runs every brand's website, with Helm, Asyst and Handbooks as the product.

content.p: Anyday's old site looked good but didn't say much. I led the redesign from the brand direction through to the final pages, repositioning Anyday from "an agency that builds websites" to the team that runs many brand websites as one system, for CTOs, CMOs and web ops leads.

ul: A moodboard and visual direction for the rebrand
A homepage concept built around one idea: one update, every site
A full page set: homepage, product pages (Helm, Asyst, Handbooks), case studies, contact and a blog
Every page in dark and light mode
A coded motion prototype so the team could review the animations before build

content.p: I started with a moodboard to set the tone: warm reds and oranges against deep black, soft blurred photography with no faces, and a serif and sans-serif pairing that felt editorial rather than techy. The references the team voted for shaped the palette and imagery.

I wanted the site to show the product's main job in a few seconds: change something once and it reaches every brand. I explored two hero concepts. In the first, a rollout card sends one shared update out to 40 sites, with the lines lighting up as the counter climbs. In the second, a file drawer of brands and pages slides in and out of a shared WebOps base. We went with the rollout.

video.caption: The final hero: one header update rolling out to every brand site

compare.caption: Homepage hero: from a brand image to a live view of what the platform does
The problem section, shown instead of told

content.p: I gave each section one idea and a small animated figure to explain it, instead of stock imagery. Hover the problem figures and the same work stacks up, the platforms split apart and the tools pile up. In the solution, the disconnected sites link up and a tile drops into one shared grid.

video.caption: The problem: three figures that animate on hover
The solution: disconnected sites connect, then one tile drops into place

content.p: I built the whole landing page as a coded motion prototype, in dark and light, so the team could scroll it, hover it and agree on the motion before development started.

compare.caption: One design, two themes, switchable from the nav

content.p: I designed one section to bring the three products together: Helm, the WebOps app for running every site in one window; Asyst, the design system every brand builds from; and Handbooks, one handbook per project.

I designed the blog as a bookshelf. The latest articles stand on the shelf as book spines next to an editor's pick; hover one and it pulls out to show the cover. Browse all lays every article out face-forward, shelf by shelf.

projects.title: Asyst Design System
projects.summary: A design system template I designed for multi-brand websites: one set of tokens, type and components every brand builds from, documented on one site.

content.p: I designed Asyst as the starting point for every new brand website. I swap the brand tokens and the whole system re-themes, while the components, rules and code stay the same.
I designed Asyst so a new brand site starts from a working system instead of a blank file, and so designers and developers work from the same tokens, components and rules.

ul: Designed the foundations: colour, typography, spacing, grid, and the logo and brand kit
Built the component library, including buttons, navigation, event cards and podcasts, each designed for desktop, tablet and mobile
Wrote usage guidelines for each component and paired it with ready-to-use code
Designed the documentation site itself, so anyone can find a component, see every state and copy the code

content.p: I documented every component the same way, and designed each one for desktop, tablet and mobile from the start.

video.caption: Moving through the component list, then the event card and navigation adapting from desktop to mobile

content.p: On every component page, I show the web and mobile versions, every state, the code to use, and the rules that keep teams from reinventing it.

projects.title: Post-Eat
projects.summary: A food-review app I designed where every review is verified at the table, and every honest review earns coins people can spend on saving the planet.

content.p: I designed Post-Eat around a simple loop: discover a restaurant, eat, scan, review, post. Reviews only count if you actually ate there, and every one earns coins you can spend on green activities, so honest reviews also do some good.

Food reviews are easy to fake and hard to trust. Anyone can rate a restaurant they've never been to, restaurants can't tell real diners from trolls, and the people who write genuinely useful reviews get nothing back for their time.
I designed the app around three ideas:

ul: Verified reviews: each restaurant has a QR code. You scan it after your meal to unlock the review, so every review comes from someone who was really there.
Rewards that matter: every review earns coins. You spend them on stickers or on sustainability activities, and your profile tracks the impact you've had.
Social discovery: a feed of reviews and short videos, search by restaurants, reviews, videos and people, and table booking in the same app.

content.p: I kept the app to five tabs: Home, Explore, Post, Rewards and Profile. Posting a review sits in the middle of the bar, because it's the one action everything else depends on.

Three onboarding screens explain the whole product: explore and share honest reviews, scan the QR code to post, and earn rewards that save the planet. I designed each one around a bright illustration, and the app launched in English and Italian, shown below.

video.caption: Onboarding, Home, Explore, Search, a video review and the profile

content.p: Explore puts hot restaurants and trending videos first. Search splits results into restaurants, reviews, videos and people, and video reviews play full-screen like the feeds people already use.
On a restaurant's page, "Post a review" opens the QR scanner. After the scan, you pick what you ate, rate it, add photos or a video and post. Coins land as soon as it's published.

I wanted people to keep reviewing because it's fun, not because they're asked to. Every review earns coins and points. Points move you up levels, from Fresh Foodie to Taste Tester to Photo Foodie, and you unlock badges as you go. Coins buy stickers you can send in chats, or go towards sustainability activities.

ul: Rewards: total coins, stickers to collect and sustainability activities to fund
Profile: contributions, followers and an Impacts tab showing the good your reviews have done
Levels, badges and stickers live on the profile, so progress is always visible

projects.title: UVS Games
projects.summary: A redesign of UVS Games — home of the UniVersus card game — with a new navigation, homepage and organized-play experience.

content.p: UVS publishes several games (UniVersus, Riftbound and Star Trek: Star Realms), but the old site hid them behind a long text menu, and the homepage was a single banner followed by a newsletter form. Players had no clear path to events, card lists or stores, so that's what I set out to fix.
I grouped Games, Discover and Hub into one mega menu, with live artwork for the game you hover.

video.caption: Mobile navigation — collapsible groups and a persistent shop button

sections.heading: A homepage that does the work

ul: Every game gets its own card with "Explore game" and "Find a store"
Latest news and upcoming events sit right on the homepage
Organized play for each game has its own banner and CTA

projects.title: Aeon Health & Shop
projects.summary: A new website for a Calgary longevity clinic, with a guided 'Start here' flow — plus an online shop for its supplements.

compare.caption: Second section — from mission statement to the patient's story

content.p: The old site listed every program in one long dropdown and didn't give new visitors an obvious first step. In my redesign, the site leads with how people feel, then guides them to that first step.

I designed the homepage to ask how you feel before it talks about programs. Eight symptom cards cover muscle changes, weight, motivation, fatigue, libido, disease prevention, gut health and brain fog. Hover a card and its video plays while a short description slides up, so people recognise themselves in a few seconds.

video.caption: Hovering through the eight symptom cards on the homepage

content.p: I created the video content on the site with Midjourney, including all eight symptom loops. Each one is a visual metaphor instead of a stock clip of a patient: glowing muscle fibres for strength, a single ember for motivation, a figure dissolving into particles for fatigue, a lone walker in fog for brain fog. They're short, muted loops, so they add motion without getting in the way.

video.caption: The eight Midjourney loops used on the symptom cards

content.p: I grouped programs and therapies by what the patient wants (hormone changes, low energy, gut and mood, long-term health, strength and recovery) instead of by clinic jargon. One click opens the full menu.

video.caption: Desktop navigation and the Programs by Symptom menu

content.p: I added a "Start here" flow that lets visitors book a free consult straight away, or take a 5-question quiz that ends with a recommended program and a way to book it.

video.caption: The quiz, from first question to recommendation

content.p: On every program page, I laid out the journey as five steps on a turning arc, from the free first call to reviewing next steps, so patients know what happens before they book.

video.caption: The What to expect steps on a program page

content.p: I also designed a companion store for Aeon's supplements, with collections by need, quick-add flavours, and subscribe-and-save on every product page.

projects.title: Agentic AI Foundation
projects.summary: The website for the Agentic AI Foundation — the Linux Foundation home of MCP, goose and AGENTS.md — rebuilt around projects, events and community.

compare.caption: aaif.io on mobile — the December 2025 launch site vs. the live redesign

content.p: The launch site introduced the foundation. With the redesign, I turned it into a hub people come back to for projects, events and community.
I designed a filterable directory of agentic AI projects, grouped by application and capability.
I made foundation events, community events and groups browsable as a grid, a calendar or a map.
I turned the hero search into a chatbot for questions like "Any upcoming events in Toronto?"

projects.title: Oxy Acne Care
projects.summary: A new store for Oxy Acne Care — a bold, Gen-Z rebrand built around "For every kind of -ne".

content.p: The old Oxy site was a straightforward product catalogue. For the relaunch, I needed to give the site a voice as bold as the new brand, and an easier way to shop by acne type.
I split the hero into Mild, Stubborn and All Acne, and each panel opens its own message and products. I built the mega menus on the same shop-by-concern logic.

projects.title: Loop Tag
projects.summary: Brand site and app for Loop Tag — QR tags that let anyone return a lost item without either person sharing personal details.

compare.caption: From a pre-launch waitlist page to the live store

content.p: Attach a tag, someone scans it, and you chat privately, with no phone number, email or address shared. My job was to make that promise obvious in seconds, on both the site and the app.
I designed two flows: owners activate and manage tags, and finders scan and message without signing up.
